newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU parliament votes to boost spending on TENs.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament votes to boost spending on TENs.

text.p: The European Parliament moved on Thursday to force the hands of European Union finance ministers to increase spending on giant European road and rail networks in a bid to boost jobs and growth.

The assembly voted for 300 million European currency units ($375 million) in the 1997 EU budget to be redistributed for trans-European transport networks, the Northern Ireland peace process, and research projects.
The move came after EU finance ministers in Luxembourg on October 14 refused to endorse a European Commission plan to spend more than $1 billion to give a jolt to the infrastructure projects.
"This is good news for the Commission," an official at the EU executive said, adding, however, that it remained to be seen how EU finance and budget ministers would react.
EU Budget Commissioner Erkki Liikanen said earlier this week he greatly appreciated the parliament's support in trying to push through priority job-creating road, rail and research projects.
Parliament was voting in a first reading of the executive European Commission's proposal for an 88-billion-Ecu budget, before a second and final reading in December.

The 14 priority projects, identified by EU leaders at a summit in Essen in December 1994, include high-speed trains between Paris and Cologne and between Frankfurt and London, plus motorways in Greece, Spain and Portugal.
The extra 1.0 billion Ecus proposed by the EU executive mainly for 1998 and 1999 would kick-start nine of the 14 projects, Commission officials say.
The reluctance of the ministers to approve additional funding stems from their all-out effort to meet the Maastricht treaty's tough criteria on budgets and debt for monetary union.
Any surplus funds in the EU budget are normally returned to national governments.
But Detlev Samland, head of the parliament's budgetary committee, said that in making budget savings the assembly wanted to help member states move towards monetary union.
"This budget...puts out signals...that we will march with them," he said.
It was now up to EU ministers to deliver the goods and agree the re-allocation of funds, he said.
Samland, a German Social Democrat, noted that the European Parliament had trimmed the budget for the first time since it was directly elected in 1979.
The road and rail networks were an integral part of Santer's confidence pact for employment, an initiative launched earlier in the year to tackle the union's mounting jobless rate.
With unemployment widely seen as the EU's most pressing problem, there is a desire within the Commission to appear responsive to the worries of the average citizen. ($1=0.80 Ecus)
